resilience: retries, timeouts and circuit breakers for TypeScript

Usage#

Run a function with retries, backoff, timeouts and cancellation through AbortSignal. Zero dependencies.

$ npm install @jondotsoy/resilience

resilience(options) builds an executor. Call .attempt() with the function you want to protect.

import { resilience } from "@jondotsoy/resilience";

const res = await resilience({ attempts: 3 }).attempt(({ signal }) =>
  fetch("https://api.example.com/data", { signal }),
);

Syntax

resilience(options).attempt((control) => T | Promise<T>): Promise<T>

Options#

Every option is optional. With no options, the function runs once. The lifecycle hooks are listed at the end of the table.

OptionTypeDefaultDescription
attemptsnumber1Number of attempts before rejecting. Must be an integer >= 1.
signalAbortSignal—Cancels the running attempt and any pending retries.
delaynumber | (ctx: DelayContext) => number0Milliseconds to wait between attempts. Pass a function to compute it per attempt. The wait is cancelled if signal is aborted.
retryable(error, ctx: RetryableContext) => boolean | Promise<boolean>retries everythingIf it returns false, rejects immediately with that error without retrying. ctx has attempt (the one that failed) and attempts.
timeoutnumber—Maximum time in ms per attempt. When it expires, control.signal is aborted and the attempt fails with a DOMException "TimeoutError", which can be retried.
fallback(lastError, ctx: FallbackContext) => F | Promise<F>—Called when the execution fails for good. Its return value becomes the result of attempt (the type becomes T | F). If it throws, attempt rejects with that error. Not called when signal is aborted.
waitForTaskbooleantrueWhat attempt does when signal is aborted or timeout expires. true: aborts control.signal and waits for the task. false: rejects right away, even if the task keeps running. See waitForTask.
Lifecycle hooks All are optional and awaited if they return a promise. If one throws, attempt rejects with that error. See Lifecycle hooks.
onStart(context: LifecycleContext) => void | Promise<void>—Before the first attempt. attempt is 0.
onAttempt(event: AttemptEvent) => void | Promise<void>—Before each attempt, including the first. Has lastError.
onTimeout(event: TimeoutEvent) => void | Promise<void>—When an attempt's timeout expires, before onError.
onError(error, context: ErrorContext) => void | Promise<void>—Every time an attempt fails. context.willRetry tells whether another follows.
onRetry(event: RetryEvent) => void | Promise<void>—Before each retry, before the wait.
onSuccess(value, context: LifecycleContext) => void | Promise<void>—When an attempt succeeds.
onFailure(error, context: LifecycleContext) => void | Promise<void>—When it fails for good, before fallback.
onAbort(reason, context: LifecycleContext) => void | Promise<void>—When signal is aborted. Neither onFailure nor fallback run.
onSettled(event: SettledEvent) => void | Promise<void>—Always, at the end, with status: "success", "fallback", "failure" or "aborted".

RetryEvent contains attempt (the attempt about to run: 2, 3, …), attempts, error (the error that caused the retry) and delay (ms to wait before running again). DelayContext contains attempt, attempts and error.

Lifecycle hooks#

Besides onRetry, the options accept on<Event> hooks that run in this order.

Scenario
onStart→
onAttempt→ onTimeout?→ onError?→ onRetry?
→ onSuccessoronFailureoronAbort →onSettled
    HookArgumentsWhen
    onStart{ attempt: 0, attempts }Before the first attempt.
    onAttempt{ attempt, attempts, lastError }Before running each attempt, including the first.
    onTimeout{ attempt, attempts, timeout }When an attempt's timeout expires (before onError).
    onError(error, { attempt, attempts, willRetry })Every time an attempt fails. willRetry tells whether another follows.
    onRetry{ attempt, attempts, error, delay }Before running again, before the wait.
    onSuccess(value, { attempt, attempts })When an attempt succeeds.
    onFailure(error, { attempt, attempts })When it fails for good, before fallback.
    onAbort(reason, { attempt, attempts })When signal is aborted. Neither onFailure nor fallback is called.
    onSettled{ status, attempt, attempts, value?, error? }Always, at the end. status is "success", "fallback", "failure" or "aborted".

    Every hook is awaited if it returns a promise. If a hook throws, attempt rejects with that error.

    await resilience({
  attempts: 3,
  timeout: 2_000,
  onAttempt: ({ attempt, attempts }) => console.log(`attempt ${attempt}/${attempts}`),
  onError: (error, { willRetry }) => console.warn("failed", error, { willRetry }),
  onSettled: ({ status, attempt }) => metrics.record("fetch_user", { status, attempt }),
}).attempt(({ signal }) => getUser(id, signal));

    Control#

    The function receives a control object on each attempt.

    FieldDescription
    signalThe attempt's AbortSignal. Pass it to fetch or any cancellable API. It is aborted when options.signal is aborted or when options.timeout expires.
    attemptNumber of the current attempt, starting at 1.
    attemptsTotal attempts allowed.
    lastErrorError from the previous attempt, or undefined on the first one.

    Behavior#

    • If the function resolves, attempt returns that value and no more attempts run.
    • If retryable returns false, it rejects with that error without further attempts.
    • If there is a fallback, any final failure (attempts exhausted or retryable returning false) resolves with whatever the fallback returns.
    • If every attempt fails and there is no fallback, attempt rejects with the error from the last attempt.
    • Between a failed attempt and the next one, onRetry is called, then it waits delay ms.
    • If options.signal is aborted during an attempt, control.signal is aborted and attempt waits for the task and returns its result or its error, without retrying. If it is aborted during the wait between attempts, it rejects right away with signal.reason. With waitForTask: false, it always rejects right away with signal.reason.

    Per-attempt vs. total timeout#

    There are two ways to set a time limit, and they can be combined.

    timeout: mssignal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms)
    What it limitsEach attempt separatelyThe whole execution, including retries and waits
    When it expiresAborts control.signal with TimeoutErrorAborts control.signal with the signal's reason
    Retried?Yes, it counts as one more failureNo, attempt rejects immediately
     
    await resilience({
  attempts: 3,
  timeout: 2_000,                      // each attempt takes at most 2 s
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000), // and everything together, at most 10 s
  delay: 500,
}).attempt(({ signal }) => fetch(url, { signal }));

    In both cases control.signal receives the abort event, so passing it to fetch or whatever API you use is enough.

    Wait for the task or not?#

    Aborting only notifies the task. If the task ignores control.signal, it may keep running. waitForTask decides what the await on .attempt() does.

    // waitForTask: false: rejects as soon as the timeout expires or the signal is aborted.
await resilience({ timeout: 1_000, waitForTask: false }).attempt(task);
// → TimeoutError after one second, even if `task` keeps running.

// Default (waitForTask: true): aborts control.signal but waits for the task to finish.
const result = await resilience({ timeout: 1_000 }).attempt(
  async ({ signal }) => {
    const items: string[] = [];
    let stop = false;

    signal.addEventListener("abort", () => {
      // signal.reason is a TimeoutError: finish the current item and stop.
      console.warn("Time is up, saving processed items", signal.reason);
      stop = true;
    });

    for (const item of queue) {
      if (stop) break;
      items.push(await process(item));
    }

    await save(items);
    return { items, complete: !stop };
  },
);

    What happens in each combination

    Limit
    waitForTask
    Task then
    task
    attempt()
    next
    ConfigurationOn expiry / abortTask succeeds afterwardsTask throws afterwardsRetries?fallback?
    timeoutAborts control.signal and waitsReturns that valueCounts as a failed attemptYesIf attempts run out
    timeout + waitForTask: falseRejects with TimeoutErrorIgnoredIgnoredYesIf attempts run out
    signalAborts control.signal and waitsReturns that valueRejects with the task's errorNoNo
    signal + waitForTask: falseRejects with signal.reasonIgnoredIgnoredNoNo

    With the default value, a task that ignores control.signal and never finishes leaves attempt waiting forever, even if timeout expires. If the task does not listen to the abort, use waitForTask: false.

    A total deadline with AbortSignal.timeout

    const result = await resilience({
  attempts: 3,
  delay: 1_000,
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
}).attempt(async ({ signal }) => {
  signal.addEventListener("abort", () => {
    // After 10 s: signal.reason is a TimeoutError.
  });
  return await longTask(signal);
});

    After 10 s, counted from when the signal was created (not from each attempt):

    • If an attempt is running, its control.signal is aborted and attempt waits for the task. If the task returns a value, attempt resolves with it (status: "success"). If it throws, attempt rejects with that error, with no retry and no fallback (status: "aborted").
    • If it is waiting between attempts, there is no task to wait for: attempt rejects right away with the TimeoutError.
    • If the signal was already aborted before calling attempt, it rejects without running the task.

    waitForTask only changes whether the running task is awaited. An aborted signal never lets a new attempt start.

    Examples#

    Report retries

    await resilience({
  attempts: 5,
  onRetry: ({ attempt, attempts, error }) => {
    console.warn(`Retry ${attempt}/${attempts}`, error);
  },
}).attempt(({ signal }) => fetch(url, { signal }));

    Wait 500 ms between attempts

    await resilience({ attempts: 3, delay: 500 }).attempt(task);

    Fallback value when everything fails

    const user = await resilience({
  attempts: 3,
  fallback: async (lastError) => {
    console.error("Could not fetch the user", lastError);
    return null;
  },
}).attempt(({ signal }) => getUser(id, signal)); // User | null

    Only retry server errors

    class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(public status: number) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}`);
  }
}

await resilience({
  attempts: 3,
  timeout: 2_000,
  retryable: (error) => !(error instanceof HttpError) || error.status >= 500,
}).attempt(async ({ signal }) => {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status);
  return res.json();
});

    Backoff#

    Ready-made helpers for the delay option. All of them accept { maxDelay, jitter }, where jitter is "full" (between 0 and the delay) or "equal" (between half the delay and the delay).

    HelperSeries with ms = 100
    fixedBackoff(ms)100, 100, 100, …
    linearBackoff(ms)100, 200, 300, …
    exponentialBackoff(ms, { factor })100, 200, 400, … (factor 2)
    fibonacciBackoff(ms)100, 100, 200, 300, 500, …

    Try the helpers below. Each bar is the wait before one retry. With jitter, the dashed outline is the computed delay and the solid bar is one random draw.

    Helper
    ms
    maxDelay
    jitter
    attempts
    6
    
        
    
          
    Every attempt fails except the last · each attempt takes 300 ms 
    
          
    
          
    0 ms
    
          
    
        
    
      
    

    import { resilience, exponentialBackoff } from "@jondotsoy/resilience";

await resilience({
  attempts: 5,
  delay: exponentialBackoff(200, { maxDelay: 5_000, jitter: "full" }),
  onRetry: ({ attempt, delay }) => console.warn(`Retry ${attempt} in ${delay} ms`),
}).attempt(task);
    
      
    You can also pass your own function: delay: ({ attempt, error }) => ….
    
      
    Every utility (backoffs, policies and errors) is also attached to the resilience function, so a single import is enough:
    

    import { resilience } from "@jondotsoy/resilience";

await resilience({
  attempts: 5,
  delay: resilience.exponentialBackoff(200, { maxDelay: 5_000 }),
}).attempt(task);

const breaker = resilience.circuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3 });
    
    
    

    
    
    
      
    Stateful policies#
    
      
    Policies keep state across calls. Create each one once, for example one per service, and share it. They all expose execute(fn) and nest with each other and with resilience.
    
      
    
        circuitBreakerStops calling a service after repeated failures, then probes it.
        bulkheadCaps how many calls run at once, with an optional queue.
        throttleAt most limit calls in a sliding window.
        cacheKeeps a result in memory for ttl ms per key.
        dedupeMerges simultaneous calls with the same key.
      
    

      
    circuitBreaker#
    
      
    After failureThreshold consecutive failures it opens and rejects instantly with CircuitOpenError. After resetTimeout ms it moves to half-open and lets one probe through: if it succeeds it closes, if it fails it opens again.
    
      
    Two consumers, A and B, share one breaker. The playground starts with an example (failureThreshold: 3, resetTimeout of 4 steps). Each button is one call to breaker.execute() where the service answers with success or failure; Wait lets a step pass with no calls. Change the options to see how the circuit reacts.
    

    
        
    
          
    failureThreshold
    3
    
          
    resetTimeout (steps)
    4
    
          
    successThreshold
    1
    
          
    
            
            
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    State
    
          
    Consecutive failures
    
          
    
            Call execute(): the service answers
            
    
              
              
              
              
              
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
        
      
    
      
      
        
    • The counter is shared. Failures from A and B add up. The third consecutive failure opens the circuit for both.
      • 
        
    • A success from either one resets the counter. B's success between A's failures brings it back to 0.
      • 
        
    • While open, neither calls the service for resetTimeout.
      • 
        
    • After that, only one call makes the probe. B's probe fails and the circuit opens again; A's later probe succeeds and the circuit closes for both.
      • 
      
    
      
    
        
    OptionDefaultDescription
    
        
          
    failureThreshold5Consecutive failures that open the circuit.
    
          
    resetTimeout30_000Ms open before probing again.
    
          
    successThreshold1Successes in half-open needed to close it.
    
          
    isFailureall(error) => boolean, which errors count as failures.
    
          
    onStateChange—(state, previous) => void.
    
            
      
    

    const breaker = circuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 5, resetTimeout: 10_000 });

await breaker.execute(() => fetch(url));
breaker.state; // "closed" | "open" | "half-open"
breaker.reset();
    

      
    bulkhead#
    

    bulkhead(options) → { execute(fn, { signal }), running, queued }
    
      
    Limits how many calls run at once. If there is a free slot, the call starts. Otherwise it waits in a queue of size maxQueue and leaves in arrival order. With every slot and the queue full, it rejects instantly with BulkheadRejectedError.
    
      
    Three consumers share one bulkhead. Each call lasts 2 steps. The playground starts with the example below (maxConcurrent: 1, maxQueue: 1). Pick who calls, press Next step, and change the limits to see how the slots and the queue behave.
    

    
        
    
          
    
            maxConcurrent
            
    1
    
          
    
          
    
            maxQueue
            
    1
    
          
    
          
    
            
            
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Running
    
          
    Queue
    
          
    
            Call execute() at the next step
            
    
              
              
              
              
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
        
      
    
      
      
        
    • The slots are shared. Among A, B and C only one call runs at a time.
      • 
        
    • B arrives while A runs and waits in the queue. C arrives in the same step, with the slot and the queue full, and is rejected.
      • 
        
    • When A finishes, B leaves the queue and starts without calling execute again. The slot is released even if the call fails.
      • 
      
    
      
    
        
    OptionDefaultDescription
    
        
          
    maxConcurrent—Calls in parallel.
    
          
    maxQueue0Calls waiting for their turn.
    
          
    signal—In execute: cancels the wait in the queue.
    
            
      
    

    const db = resilience.bulkhead({
  maxConcurrent: 2,
  maxQueue: 1,
});

export const query = (sql: string, signal?: AbortSignal) =>
  db.execute(() => client.query(sql), { signal });

db.running; // running
db.queued;  // waiting
    

      
    throttle#
    

    throttle(options) → { execute(fn), remaining }
    
      
    At most limit calls in any span of interval ms. When exceeded it rejects with ThrottleError, whose retryAfter says how many ms remain until a slot frees up. Rejected calls do not use up slots.
    
      
    Three consumers share one throttle. The playground starts with an example (limit: 3, interval of 5 steps). Pick who calls, press Next step, and change the limits to see how the sliding window fills and frees up.
    

    
        
    
          
    limit
    3
    
          
    interval (steps)
    5
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Window
    
          
    remaining
    
          
    
            Call execute() at the next step
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
        
      
    
      
      
        
    • The limit is shared. A, B and C use the 3 slots in the first step, so the next tries from A and B do not call the service.
      • 
        
    • Each ThrottleError carries retryAfter: the time left until the oldest call leaves the window.
      • 
        
    • The window is sliding: at each step, the calls from the last 5 steps count.
      • 
      
    
      
    
        
    OptionDefaultDescription
    
        
          
    limit—Calls allowed per window.
    
          
    interval—Window size in ms.
    
            
      
    

    const api = resilience.throttle({
  limit: 3,
  interval: 1_000, // 3 per second
});

try {
  await api.execute(() => fetch(url));
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof resilience.ThrottleError) {
    console.log("retry in", error.retryAfter, "ms");
  }
}
    

      
    cache#
    

    cache(options) → { execute(key, fn), delete(key), clear(), size }
    
      
    Stores the result of fn in memory for a key during ttl ms, counted from when the value arrives. A request that arrives while the first call is still in flight shares that execution. Errors are not cached.
    
      
    Three consumers request the same key. The service takes 2 steps to respond. The playground starts with an example (ttl of 5 steps). Pick who calls, choose whether the next service call succeeds or fails, and press Next step. delete(key) invalidates the entry.
    

    
        
    
          
    ttl (steps)
    5
    
          
    Next service call
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Entry for the key
    
          
    
            Call execute("config") at the next step
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
        
      
    
      
    
        
    OptionDefaultDescription
    
        
          
    ttl—Lifetime of each entry in ms.
    
          
    maxSizeunlimitedMaximum entries. When exceeded, the oldest is evicted.
    
            
      
    

    const users = resilience.cache({
  ttl: 60_000,
  maxSize: 500,
});

export const getUser = (id: string) =>
  users.execute(`user:${id}`, () => fetchUser(id));

users.delete("user:42"); // invalidate an entry
    

      
    dedupe#
    

    dedupe() → { execute(key, fn), pending }
    
      
    If a call with the same key is already in flight, it returns that same promise instead of running fn again. It does not store results: as soon as the call finishes, the key is released. Useful when several components request the same thing at once, like the configuration at startup.
    
      
    Three consumers request the same key, and the service takes 2 steps to respond. Pick who calls and press Next step: whoever arrives while a call is in flight gets the same promise, and the key is free again as soon as it settles.
    

    
        
    
          
          
    Next service call
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
    Key
    
          
    
            Call execute("config") at the next step
            
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
        
    
        
      
    
      
    Unlike cache, dedupe only merges simultaneous requests. To reuse the value after it arrives, use cache.
    

    const inFlight = resilience.dedupe();

// A, B and C call almost at once: a single request
const [a, b, c] = await Promise.all([
  inFlight.execute("config", loadConfig),
  inFlight.execute("config", loadConfig),
  inFlight.execute("config", loadConfig),
]);
    

      
    Combining policies#
    
      
    The nesting order defines the behavior. A breaker on the outside makes the whole retry sequence count as a single call:
    

    const breaker = circuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 3 });
const pool = bulkhead({ maxConcurrent: 10 });

const getData = () =>
  breaker.execute(() =>
    resilience({
      attempts: 3,
      timeout: 2_000,
      delay: exponentialBackoff(200),
    }).attempt(({ signal }) => pool.execute(() => fetch(url, { signal }), { signal })),
  );

// With a fallback on the outside, even a CircuitOpenError ends in the fallback value:
const getDataSafe = () =>
  resilience({ fallback: () => cachedData }).attempt(getData);
    
    
    

    
    
    
      
    Build a decorator#
    
      
    resilience does not ship a decorator, but you can build one in a few lines with TypeScript 5 standard decorators (no experimentalDecorators), which Bun also supports.
    
      
    1. The decorator
    
      
    It creates the executor once and replaces the method with one that runs inside attempt. The attempt's control is appended as the last argument.
    

    import { resilience, type Control, type ResilienceOptions } from "@jondotsoy/resilience";

export function resilient<This>(
  options: ResilienceOptions | ((self: This) => ResilienceOptions) = {},
) {
  return function <Args extends unknown[], R>(
    method: (this: This, ...args: [...Args, Control?]) => R | Promise<R>,
    _context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext<This>,
  ) {
    // With fixed options, a single executor for every instance.
    const shared = typeof options === "function" ? undefined : resilience(options);

    return function (this: This, ...args: Args): Promise<R> {
      const r =
        shared ?? resilience((options as (self: This) => ResilienceOptions)(this));
      return r.attempt((control) => method.call(this, ...args, control));
    };
  };
}
    
      
    2. Use it in a class
    
      
    Declare control as the last, optional parameter. Callers do not pass it: the decorator supplies it on each attempt.
    

    class UsersApi {
  @resilient({
    attempts: 3,
    timeout: 2_000,
    delay: resilience.exponentialBackoff(200),
  })
  async getUser(id: string, control?: Control) {
    const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`, {
      signal: control?.signal,
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    return res.json();
  }
}

const user = await new UsersApi().getUser("42");
    
      
    3. Per-instance options
    
      
    If each object has its own AbortController, pass a function that receives the instance. The executor is then created on every call.
    

    class Worker {
  readonly abort = new AbortController();

  @resilient((self: Worker) => ({ attempts: 3, signal: self.abort.signal }))
  async process(job: Job, control?: Control) {
    // ...
  }

  close() {
    this.abort.abort();
  }
}
    
      
    4. Add stateful policies
    
      
    Create policies outside the class so every instance shares them, then use them inside the method with execute.
    

    const breaker = resilience.circuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 5 });

class PaymentsApi {
  @resilient({ attempts: 3, delay: resilience.exponentialBackoff(200) })
  async charge(order: Order, control?: Control) {
    return breaker.execute(() =>
      fetch("https://payments.example.com/charge", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify(order),
        signal: control?.signal,
      }),
    );
  }
}
    
      
    
        
    control always goes last, after the arguments the caller passed. If optional parameters before it are omitted, it lands in a different position, so prefer fixed parameters or an options object. With fixed options, the configuration is shared by every instance. The decorated method always returns a promise.
